text: Εἰς στηλογραφίαν. Assumit Maximus proclivi Græcorum usu, ut quasi ex titulo proscriptionem significet, seu damnationem (nempe malitiæ vitiique) factam primo in Christo, exque illo, ac per illum in sanctis. Potius tamen (hic præcipue) titulum victoriæ Christi videatur sonare. Habetur eadem vox Psal. xv, lv, lvi, lviii, ubi οἱ LXX sic reddentes, aliud videntur legisse quam modo Hebræa habeant : nempe מכתב, non ut jam legimus מכתם, quod Arabica voce rem absconditam significat, id est, servatu dignam, nisi etiam sic reddendo servandi modum explicare voluerunt, ut scilicet perenni titulo ad memoriam servetur, ac velut columnæ inscriptum. Sic sæpe illi, paulo aliter reddendo, non alias voces legerunt, sed ut eas ipsas, quas legimus, clarioribus aliis redderent, sibi indulserunt. Quidam instrumentum musicum volunt : alii insigne militare; cum ejus radix sit כתם, quæ auri optimi massam significat. Chald. exemplar, quod ipsum a tituli inscriptione non valde remotum, adjuncta præsertim voce εἰς διδαχήν, in documentum.
anchorLine: στηλογραφίαν (a) δὲ τῷ Δαβίδ· τουτέστιν, αὐτῷ
en: On 'Eis stelographian' (for a stele-inscription): Maximus takes up the Greek habit, in which the word signifies, as it were, a proscription or condemnation (of wickedness and vice) first carried out in Christ, and from him and through him in the saints. Yet the title seems rather to sound a victory of Christ. The same word occurs at Pss. 15, 55, 56, 58, where the LXX, translating thus, seem to have read something other than what the Hebrew now has: that is, mktb, not mktm as we now read, which in Arabic means a hidden thing, that is, worthy of being kept; unless by this rendering they also meant to express the manner of keeping, namely that it be kept in memory by a perpetual title, as inscribed on a column. So they often, rendering a little differently, did not read other words but allowed themselves to render the very words we read by clearer ones. Some take it for a musical instrument, others for a military standard, since its root is ktm, which means a mass of finest gold. Chaldee: 'exemplar', which is not far from the sense of the title, especially with the added phrase 'for teaching', 'for instruction'.

text: Τὴν Συρίαν Σωβά. Sic emendo, quod ita sequentibus codices habeant, non Σοβάλ, quod liquet non reddidisse τοὺς LXX, ut nec Hebræa habent, sed idipsum quod II Reg. et I Par. Ubique enim צובה, cum Sobal longe alia vox sit, aliudque significet, atque aliis prorsus litteris Hebraice scribatur, nempe שובל, uti et qua septem significant, שבע, mirumque venisse in mentem Maximo, sive ei, qui illi auctor etymi fuit, ut Soba septem interpretaretur; cum sit clare exercitus, militans, etc.
anchorLine: ὅταν ἐνεπύρισε τὴν Μεσοποταμίαν, καὶ (b) τὴν Συ-
en: 'Ten Syrian Soba': thus I emend, because the codices so have it in what follows, not 'Sobal', which clearly the LXX did not render, as the Hebrew texts do not have it either, but the same as II Kings and I Chronicles. For everywhere it is tsobah, since Sobal is a far different word, signifies something else, and is written in Hebrew with quite other letters, namely shobal; so too the word meaning 'seven' is sheva. It is strange that it came into Maximus's mind, or that of whoever supplied him the etymology, to interpret Soba as 'seven', when it clearly means 'host, army, warring', etc.

text: Λύων ἰσχύν. Nempe legit Maximus, seu qui illi præivit etymologistes הדדעזר, quasi a חדד, languidus, sicque scribitur, II Reg. viii; etsi I Paral. xviii, est ד loco ר pro tertia littera. Possit et a הדד amicum auxilium. Auctor explicationis propriorum nominum Biblicorum, per ר et ח legit.
anchorLine: Λύων ἰσχὺν (c)  [call stands at foot of p-0432, Greek column, last line]
en: 'Lyon ischyn' (destroying strength): Maximus reads thus, or whoever preceded him as etymologist, reading Hadadezer as if from Hadad, 'languid'; and so it is written at II Kings 8, though I Chronicles 18 has a dalet in place of a resh as the third letter. It could also be from Hadad, 'friendly help'. The author of the explanation of Biblical proper names read it with resh and het.

text: Ὠμίασις. שכם humerus est, ὠμίας· qui latis humeris est, Poll. l. iii, c. 30, unde sibi Maximus eam vocem habuit. Est autem humerus virtutis symbolum, quod athletæ eorum maxime firmitate victoria potiuntur, et quod sint ferendo onera.
anchorLine: δρικοὺς τῶν ἀρετῶν τρόπους. Ὠμίασις (d) γὰρ ἡ
en: 'Omiasis': shkm (Hebrew) means 'shoulder', Greek 'omias', one who has broad shoulders (Pollux, book 3, chapter 30), whence Maximus took the word. The shoulder is a symbol of virtue, because athletes win victory chiefly by the firmness of the shoulders, and because burdens are to be borne.

text: Τὴν κοιλάδα τῶν Σκηνῶν. Videatur in vi potius nominis proprii accipi, quod ita singulariter vallis Tabernaculorum dicitur סכות, quod forte locus in Syria paulo humilior et populosissimus, ut Syria pro vastitate regionis, alia aliaque induebat nomina. Sic passim in regionibus alta et depressa dividimus; montana et convalles, quarum fere major fertilitas, ac proinde incolarum frequentia. Nec forte alia sit vallis Succot, quam vallis ipsa Salis, quam notiori nomine significare voluerit, qui titulum psalmo apposuit, vel Esdras, vel ipse David. Campestrium crebra mentio in Veteri Instrumento, ubi vel itinera narrantur vel prœlia.
anchorLine: Καὶ τὴν κοιλάδα τῶν Σκηνῶν (e) διαμετρεῖ· τοὺς
en: 'The valley of the tents': it seems to be taken rather as a proper name, since it is singularly called the 'valley of Tabernacles' (sukkot), which perhaps is a place in Syria somewhat lower and very populous; Syria, because of the devastation of the region, took on one name after another. So we commonly divide regions into high and low, mountains and valleys, of which the latter are generally more fertile and so more densely populated. Nor perhaps is the valley of Succoth other than the very 'valley of Salt', which the one who put the title on the psalm, whether Ezra or David himself, wished to signify by the better-known name. Mention of plains is frequent in the Old Testament, where either journeys or battles are narrated.

text: Κραταίωσις. Psal. cvii, 9, ubi eadem vox Hebraica, iidemque repetiti versus, est ἀντίληψις 'auxilium, susceptio, quam utramque vocem Maximus exponit; cum sit sola variatio interpretis. Ephraim quod πλατυσμὸς redditur, intelligatur ampla progenie secundum quod fructificare significat et fecundum esse.
en: 'Krataiosis' (strengthening): Psalm 107:9, where the same Hebrew word and the same repeated verses occur, has antilepsis, 'help, support', both of which words Maximus explains; the only variation is the translator's. Ephraim, which is rendered 'platysmos' (enlargement), is to be understood as ample progeny, according to the verb meaning to bear fruit and be fruitful.

text: Ἔντερον πατρός. באב simplicius a patre, quod incesto concubitu ex patre susceptus, Gen. xix, 37, mutato tzere in vau cholem.
en: 'Enteron patros' (bowel of the father): the Hebrew (mo'av), more simply 'from the father', because he was conceived of his father by incestuous intercourse (Gen. 19:37), the tsere having been changed to vav-holem.

text: Αἱματώδης πηλός. אדם, rubere, rubrum esse, ruber, homo, terra rubri seu argillacei coloris, ex qua et nomen homini inditum, quod de illa formatus sit.
en: 'Haimatodes pelos' (blood-red clay): the Hebrew adom means 'to be red, to be red-coloured', 'red', 'man', 'earth of a red or clay colour', from which the name was also given to man, because he was formed from it.
